steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
A transformer is a type of neural network architecture especially well suited for processing sequences (text, speech, etc.) by letting every position in the sequence “attend” to every other position. Conceptually it works in these stages:

1. Input Embedding and Positional Encoding  
   • Each token (word, subword, etc.) is mapped to a continuous vector (“embedding”).  
   • Since self-attention itself is permutation-invariant, a fixed or learned positional encoding is added so the model knows the order of tokens.

2. Self-Attention Mechanism  
   • For each position in the sequence, compute three vectors by multiplying the embedding by learned weight matrices: a Query (Q), a Key (K), and a Value (V).  
   • Compute attention scores between position i and j by taking the dot product Qi·Kj and scaling (divide by √d).  
   • Normalize the scores across all j with a softmax to get attention weights.  
   • The new representation at position i is the weighted sum of all Vj, using those attention weights.  
   This lets each token dynamically gather information from all others in the sequence.

3. Multi-Head Attention  
   • Rather than doing one big QKV projection, perform several smaller “heads” in parallel (e.g. 8 or 16).  
   • Each head learns a different way to attend.  
   • The outputs of all heads are concatenated and linearly projected back to the model dimension.  
   This increases the model’s capacity to capture diverse relationships.

4. Position-wise Feed-Forward Network  
   • After attention, each position (independently) passes through a small two-layer fully connected network (same weights for every position).  
   • Typically: linear → activation (ReLU or GeLU) → linear.

5. Residual Connections and Layer Normalization  
   • Around both the multi-head attention block and the feed-forward block, add the input back to the output (residual or skip connection).  
   • Apply layer normalization (stabilizes and speeds up training).

6. Stacking Layers  
   • A transformer encoder stacks N copies of [Multi-Head Attention → Add & Norm → Feed-Forward → Add & Norm].  
   • In a full encoder-decoder transformer (e.g. original “Attention Is All You Need”), the decoder adds masked self-attention and cross-attention to the encoder outputs.

7. Output Projection  
   • In language models, the topmost transformer layer’s output vectors are projected onto the vocabulary size and turned into probabilities via softmax.  
   • During training, you compare those probabilities to the true next token. During inference, you sample or take the argmax.

Key Intuitions  
 • Global Context: Unlike RNNs which propagate information step by step, self-attention lets every token look at every other token in parallel.  
 • Parallelism: All positions can be processed simultaneously, so training and inference are much faster on modern hardware.  
 • Flexibility: By stacking many layers of attention and feed-forward blocks, the model builds up increasingly abstract representations of the input.

In short, a transformer transforms raw token embeddings into context-aware representations by repeated rounds of attending to every part of the sequence, mixing that information via feed-forward networks, and stabilizing via residuals and normalization.
